messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Workplace: Workplace, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations, Overwork: work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts
  Threat: Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Vignette:
Darnell, a 62-year-old African American man, had spent most of his adult life in bomb disposal work, a profession he once described with pride as exacting and necessary, the sort of job that demanded calm hands and absolute concentration. The incident that changed that steadiness came during a response to a suspected chemical device at work, when a toxic exposure left him abruptly overwhelmed by the smell and the physical reality of something in the air that was not supposed to be there. He remembered the scene in fragments: the worksite, the urgency, the clatter and shouted instructions around him, then the sudden tightening in his chest and the unmistakable sense that his body had been placed in danger before he had fully understood what was happening. In the months that followed, Darnell found that ordinary loud noises could send a jolt through him, especially sharp bangs at work that sounded too much like the abrupt violence of that day. The smell of hospitals or antiseptic also became difficult for him to tolerate; if he passed through a clinic corridor or caught that clean, medicinal odor in a medical setting, his attention narrowed and he felt pulled back to the period when he was being checked and monitored after the exposure.

He began changing the way he moved through daily life almost without noticing it at first. At work, he was still highly functional, but he overworked himself, taking on extra tasks and staying busy well beyond what was required because he did not like the moments between demands, when his thoughts had room to catch up with him. He had come to rely on constant activity as a way to keep from being alone in a room or building, and he disliked the silence that settled when a job ended and everyone else had gone home. If he finished late and found himself alone in the workplace, he would keep busy with paperwork or minor checks, preferring the structure of motion to the unease of sitting still. He also avoided hospitals, ambulances, and physical examinations whenever he could. Medical settings felt especially difficult after the exposure, and he would rearrange appointments or delay care unless something made it impossible to postpone. His avoidance had practical consequences: he was less willing to seek routine medical attention, and the prospect of being examined in a clinical room, under fluorescent lights with that antiseptic smell, was enough to make him tense before he even arrived.

What Darnell noticed most in the present was how much of his attention now went to keeping ahead of danger. He constantly scanned his surroundings for signs of it, even in places where he knew, rationally, that nothing was likely to happen. When he entered a building, he immediately identified escape routes before he felt comfortable enough to settle, mentally mapping exits, hallways, and the fastest way out. He did this in restaurants, at work, and even in his own family’s social gatherings, where he would choose a seat that let him see the door. His wife had learned that he preferred to stand rather than sit for long periods in unfamiliar spaces, and that he often positioned himself near an exit without explaining why. He was also startled when someone touched him unexpectedly. A hand on his shoulder from behind, a casual tap from a coworker, or even an affectionate gesture caught him off guard could make him react with visible alarm before he had time to compose himself, as if his body responded before his mind could catch up. He found these reactions embarrassing, but they seemed to him unavoidable, the kind of reflex that arrived fully formed and left him trying to regain his composure.

By the time he came for help, Darnell had become tired of organizing his days around staying alert and staying busy. He could still do his work, but it had become harder to ignore how much effort it took to maintain that pace and how often he found himself planning routes, checking surroundings, and bracing for unexpected contact or noise. He spoke as someone who did not want to lose his competence or his place in the world, yet who was increasingly weary of living as though he were always one moment away from danger. What finally brought him in was the sense that these patterns had narrowed his life enough that even a man trained for high-risk situations no longer felt fully at ease in ordinary ones. He wanted relief, though he was also worried that if he stopped working so much or let himself be still, the thoughts and sensations he had been outrunning would come rushing in.
